lead: Every two-port parameter set is the same pair of linear equations, solved for a different pair of variables. So one set follows from another by algebra, with no new measurement. This matters every day: a transistor data sheet gives h parameters but a cascade needs ABCD; a series connection needs Z but the network was measured as Y. The conversion is exact whenever the parameter it divides by is not zero; when it is zero, the target set does not exist for that network.
prereq: You need Z and Y parameters, h and g parameters, ABCD parameters, and 2 × 2 determinants.

blocks.text: Write the known set, solve one of its equations for the variable that the target set wants on the right, and substitute into the other equation. Here is Z to ABCD, the derivation examiners ask for most.

items: Start from V₁ = z₁₁I₁ + z₁₂I₂ and V₂ = z₂₁I₁ + z₂₂I₂. ABCD wants V₁ and I₁ in terms of V₂ and −I₂.
Solve the second equation for I₁: I₁ = (1/z₂₁)V₂ − (z₂₂/z₂₁)I₂. Comparing with I₁ = CV₂ − DI₂ gives C = 1/z₂₁ and D = z₂₂/z₂₁.
Substitute I₁ into the first equation: V₁ = (z₁₁/z₂₁)V₂ − (z₁₁z₂₂/z₂₁)I₂ + z₁₂I₂ = (z₁₁/z₂₁)V₂ − (Δz/z₂₁)I₂.
Compare with V₁ = AV₂ − BI₂: A = z₁₁/z₂₁ and B = Δz/z₂₁, where Δz = z₁₁z₂₂ − z₁₂z₂₁.
Every term divides by z₂₁, so the conversion needs z₂₁ ≠ 0.

blocks.text: The other conversions come the same way, or by matrix inversion where the two sets swap all four variables: [Y] = [Z]⁻¹ and [g] = [h]⁻¹. The determinants that appear are Δz (Ω²), Δy (S²), Δh and Δg (no unit) and Δ<sub>T</sub> = AD − BC (no unit).
Each row gives one parameter in terms of each of the other sets. Read across a row, never down a column.

Each entry was checked by converting a test network through every route and comparing. The g set is the inverse of h: g₁₁ = h₂₂/Δh, g₁₂ = −h₁₂/Δh, g₂₁ = −h₂₁/Δh, g₂₂ = h₁₁/Δh. Some syllabi call this topic the interrelationships between parameter sets.

items: Units: z in Ω, y in S, h₁₁ in Ω, h₂₂ in S, B in Ω, C in S; h₁₂, h₂₁, A and D have none. A B in siemens means a row was misread.
Reciprocity: z₁₂ = z₂₁ must come out as y₁₂ = y₂₁, h₁₂ = −h₂₁ and Δ<sub>T</sub> = 1. In general Δ<sub>T</sub> = z₁₂/z₂₁, so this is a one-line check on any Z-to-ABCD result.

Zero divisors: the Z column needs Δz ≠ 0 for Y and z₂₂ ≠ 0 for h; the ABCD row needs z₂₁ ≠ 0. A network with z₂₁ = 0 (no forward transmission, a unilateral network) has y₂₁ = h₂₁ = 0 too, so it has no ABCD matrix by any route. Work with its Z, Y or h equations directly.
A second route is a free check: compute the target from two different known sets and compare, as the first worked example does.

examples.question: A transistor has h₁₁ = 1 kΩ, h₁₂ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴, h₂₁ = 50 and h₂₂ = 25 μS. Find its Z parameters, then its ABCD parameters, and check the ABCD set by the direct h-to-ABCD row.
steps: Δ<sub>T</sub> = AD − BC = 5 × 10⁻⁶ − 10⁻⁵ = −5 × 10⁻⁶ = z₁₂/z₂₁, not 1: an active device is not reciprocal.
examples.answer: z₁₁ = 500 Ω, z₁₂ = 10 Ω, z₂₁ = −2 MΩ, z₂₂ = 40 kΩ; A = −2.5 × 10⁻⁴, B = −20 Ω, C = −5 × 10⁻⁷ S, D = −0.02, the same by both routes.

examples.question: The π network of 2 Ω (shunt at port 1), 4 Ω (series) and 5 Ω (shunt at port 2) has y₁₁ = 0.75 S, y₁₂ = y₂₁ = −0.25 S and y₂₂ = 0.45 S. Convert to h parameters and check h₁₁ and h₂₂ from the circuit.
steps: Check h₁₁: with port 2 shorted, the 5 Ω is shorted out and port 1 sees 2 ∥ 4 = 8/6 = 1.3333 Ω ✓.
Check h₂₂: with port 1 open, port 2 sees 5 ∥ (4 + 2) = 30/11 = 2.7273 Ω, an admittance of 0.3667 S ✓. Also h₁₂ = −h₂₁, as the network is reciprocal.

traps: [Y] = [Z]⁻¹ is a matrix inverse: y₁₁ = z₂₂/Δz, not 1/z₁₁. For the T network 1/z₁₁ = 0.1667 S but y₁₁ = 0.2692 S.
Signs in the table are part of the formula. h₂₁ = −z₂₁/z₂₂ is negative for a passive network; dropping the minus gives a passive network with current gain, which is impossible.
z₂₁ = 0 means no ABCD matrix exists by any route; it is not a reason to try another row of the table.
Δh and Δ<sub>T</sub> have no unit, Δz is in Ω² and Δy in S². Quote the unit of every converted parameter.
Reciprocity checks the arithmetic only for a passive network. An active device such as the transistor gives Δ<sub>T</sub> ≠ 1 even when every step is right.

quiz.q: Write h₁₁ and h₂₁ in terms of Z parameters.
quiz.a: h₁₁ = Δz/z₂₂ and h₂₁ = −z₂₁/z₂₂, with Δz = z₁₁z₂₂ − z₁₂z₂₁.

quiz.q: Why can the same two-port be described by Z, Y, h, g and ABCD without any new measurement?
quiz.a: Each set is the same two linear equations in V₁, I₁, V₂, I₂, solved for a different pair. Solving one form for another pair gives the other set, so the behaviour at the ports is unchanged.

quiz.q: A two-port has z₁₁ = 10 Ω, z₁₂ = 2 Ω, z₂₁ = 5 Ω, z₂₂ = 8 Ω. Find A, B, C, D and Δ<sub>T</sub>.
quiz.a: Δz = 80 − 10 = 70 Ω². A = 10/5 = 2; B = 70/5 = 14 Ω; C = 1/5 = 0.2 S; D = 8/5 = 1.6. Δ<sub>T</sub> = 3.2 − 2.8 = 0.4 = z₁₂/z₂₁ = 2/5, so the network is not reciprocal.

quiz.q: Convert the T network's ABCD parameters (1.5, 6.5 Ω, 0.25 S, 1.75) to Y parameters.
quiz.a: y₁₁ = D/B = 1.75/6.5 = 0.2692 S; y₁₂ = −Δ<sub>T</sub>/B = −1/6.5 = −0.1538 S; y₂₁ = −1/B = −0.1538 S; y₂₂ = A/B = 1.5/6.5 = 0.2308 S. These match the Y parameters found by inverting [Z].

quiz.q: Find the ABCD parameters of the π network from its Y parameters (0.75, −0.25, −0.25, 0.45 S).
A two-port has z₂₁ = 0. What does this mean physically, and which sets can still describe it?
quiz.a: Current into port 1 produces no voltage at port 2: there is no forward transmission. Then y₂₁ = h₂₁ = 0 as well and every ABCD formula divides by zero, so no ABCD matrix exists. Its Z set (and Y or h, if their determinants allow) still describes it.

quiz.q: A student converts Z to Y by writing y₁₁ = 1/z₁₁ and y₂₂ = 1/z₂₂. When, if ever, is this right?
quiz.a: Only when z₁₂z₂₁ = 0, so that Δz = z₁₁z₂₂. In general the off-diagonal terms enter through Δz: y₁₁ = z₂₂/Δz.

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators and RF tools convert between Z, Y, ABCD and S parameters automatically, using the same algebra with complex numbers at each frequency; S parameters use a reference impedance, usually 50 Ω. Search for “S parameter to ABCD conversion” and “two-port parameter conversion table”.
